CrewPulse is a research prototype for astronaut self-assessment, built for NASA Space Apps 2026 by team KHNUIA. It is not a medical device and does not replace a flight surgeon. Thresholds come from NASA HRP, NASA-STD-3001 and peer-reviewed sources.
Earth can answer in ~%1$.0f min, longer than the %2$.0f-min response window. The crew medical officer leads; a report is queued for the flight surgeon.
Earth can answer in ~%1$.0f min, within the response window. Start the onboard actions while waiting.

What to do, step by step
Stop the current task and sit down. Do not stay alone.
Call the crew medical officer now. They lead with the onboard protocol and the medical kit.
Re-measure the red value now and then every 15 minutes.
A report is queued for Earth; the reply arrives in ~%1$.0f min. Do not wait for it to act.
Contact the flight surgeon on Earth now. The reply arrives in ~%1$.0f min.
While waiting, start the advice for the red value (below) together with the crew medical officer.
Re-measure the flagged values below to rule out a measurement error.
Tell the crew medical officer which systems are flagged and their values. Not urgent, but today.
Follow the advice for each flagged value (see below).
Re-check tomorrow morning. If it gets worse or you feel unwell, the status turns red.
Re-measure as planned in today’s mission.
Keep the daily routine and today’s measurements.
Flagged values and what to do
Chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, confusion or fever above 38 °C: tell the crew medical officer immediately, whatever the app shows.
Earth response: signal %1$.0f min one way, %2$.0f min there and back, plus %3$.0f min for the doctor to read and answer = %4$.0f min.
Response window: a red value needs a response within 30 minutes (Australasian Triage Scale, category 3).
Response window: a yellow value should be reviewed within 24 hours.
Response window: everything is green, nothing needs a response.
Rule: if Earth answers slower than the window, the crew acts on its own with the onboard protocol.
allowed only with extra checks: re-measure first, a second crew member nearby
not allowed until the reasons above are fixed
Day %1$d of a ~%2$d-day transfer to Mars (a Mars transfer usually takes 6–9 months). The signal needs %3$.0f min one way, so Earth always answers with a delay.
The signal to Earth needs %1$.0f min one way.
All of today’s measurements are done
Seated, arm at heart level, after 5 minutes of rest. Use the onboard cuff before exercise.

Microgravity shifts fluids toward the head and deconditions the heart and vessels. Blood pressure regulation changes in flight and after landing. Bands follow AHA categories: 120-129 (elevated) stays green, yellow starts at stage 1 hypertension (130), red at stage 2 (140) or hypotension (below 90).
No action. Keep the daily routine.
Repeat the measurement in 1 hour. Reduce salt, keep hydration and planned cardio exercise.
Repeat now. If confirmed, report to the crew medical officer and log for the flight surgeon.
Taken together with systolic pressure, same conditions.
See systolic blood pressure: fluid shift and cardiovascular deconditioning.
Repeat in 1 hour, review hydration and stress.
Repeat now. If confirmed, report to the crew medical officer.
Right after waking, before getting out of the sleep station. Wearable, finger sensor or the camera pulse scan.
A resting heart rate well above your own baseline can signal deconditioning, poor sleep, infection or stress.
Check sleep and hydration. Re-measure tomorrow morning.
Re-measure now. With symptoms (dizziness, chest pain) report to the crew medical officer immediately.
Finger-stick glucometer before breakfast, after at least 8 hours without food.
Reduced physical load and stress hormones can change insulin sensitivity during long missions.
Below 70: eat 15 g of fast carbohydrates and re-test in 15 minutes. 100-125: review diet and exercise adherence, re-test in 2 days.
Below 54: eat 15 g of fast carbohydrates now, re-test in 15 minutes and tell a crewmate. 126 or above: re-test fasting and report.
Oral or ear thermometer, at rest, not right after exercise.

Spaceflight alters the immune response and can reactivate latent viruses. Fever is an early sign. Core body temperature of astronauts also rises by about 1 °C on long missions, so compare with your own in-flight baseline.
Report to the crew medical officer. Limit contact with crewmates if infection is suspected.
Self-report or wearable: total sleep time last night.
Shifted light-dark cycles, noise and workload cut sleep on missions. Sleep loss reduces alertness and performance.
Keep a fixed sleep window, dim screens 1 hour before sleep.
Two nights in a row: tell the commander, avoid critical tasks without a cross-check, run the PVT test.
Self-rating from 1 (very low) to 5 (very good), same time every day.
Isolation and confinement are one of the five hazards of human spaceflight and affect behavioral health.
Schedule a private call with family or a psychologist, plan leisure time.
Several days in a row: talk to the crew medical officer and the ground behavioral health team.
3-minute reaction test in the app. Same time of day each run.

Slower reactions are an objective sign of fatigue or sleep loss, before you notice it yourself. Yellow starts when the average response reaches the 3-minute PVT-B lapse threshold (355 ms), red at the classic 10-minute PVT lapse threshold (500 ms).
Postpone non-urgent precision tasks, take a short rest.
Do not perform critical tasks alone. Report fatigue to the commander.
Personal dosimeter reading, summed over the mission.

NASA limits career effective dose to 600 mSv and requires doses as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA). Yellow starts at half of the limit, red at 90% of it. Beyond Earth\'s magnetic field the daily dose rises several times.
Minimize time in low-shielded modules, sleep in the shielded quarters.
Close to the career limit: mission control must review EVA and activity plans.
Short sleep, slower reactions and low mood together point to accumulated fatigue.
Protect the next sleep window, avoid critical tasks without a cross-check, re-run the PVT tomorrow.
Raised temperature together with a resting heart rate above your baseline.
Rest, fluids, re-measure temperature in 4 hours, tell the crew medical officer.
Blood pressure and resting heart rate are both elevated or drifting upward.
Repeat measurements tomorrow morning, review salt and fluid intake, keep planned cardio exercise.
Self-report does not match the data
You rate your mood as good, but objective signs of strain disagree. People under pressure tend to underrate symptoms.
Take an honest second look at how you feel. Consider a private check-in with the crew medical officer.
Bone fracture due to spaceflight-induced bone changes
Sleep loss, circadian desynchronization and work overload
